rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its line, "Without a bank willing to be identified, this becomes a claim the reporter cannot check," is the adult in the room; B's "Notion shipping offline mode in 2026 is an admission the always-online SaaS bet had a ceiling" turns a product feature into a think-piece thesis the facts do not support. B has sharper-looking wrappers, but two of them need invented industry norms to stand up.
gaps_in_A: "bank and hospital compliance" over-specifies healthcare into hospitals. The update says healthcare buyers, not hospitals or health systems.
"It just shipped the checklist" is a little too tidy. CMEK, residency, and offline are controls, but no actual compliance checklist or certification is supplied.

"How Notion made a shared editor work with no connection at all" is a viable engineering angle, but the conflict-resolution story is inferred and would collapse without an engineer giving real architecture detail.
gaps_in_B: "after it agreed to hand over the keys" is cute and sloppy. CMEK via AWS KMS is not Notion "handing over" keys, and "agreed" implies negotiation not in evidence.
"as sovereignty demands spread" invents a broader trend from one product launch. No regulatory event or market evidence was supplied.
"an admission the always-online SaaS bet had a ceiling" is pure columnist cologne. The facts say offline editing shipped; they do not prove an industry reversal or confession.
"without raising prices, cutting against the security-upsell norm" overreads "no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans" and imports a competitor-pricing thesis the update does not prove.
